cards.tip: FIX — When the customer offered his own theory about the problem, David decided to verify it first, but asking what he suspected and presenting the rust corrosion finding he'd already discovered would have kept momentum toward building options instead of pausing for the report.
FIX — Clearly explain findings and give customers a framework for next steps.
FIX — Create clear options and set expectations for the next steps in the process.
FIX — After diagnosis, build options and reconnect to customer's stated concerns.
FIX — Build specific options with pricing and timelines after diagnosis.
FIX — This appears to be findings presentation; ensure customer understood options.
FIX — Present multiple options and reconnect solutions to the customer's original concerns.
FIX — Build options and present multiple paths forward rather than just diagnosis.

WIN — When customer hesitated about investing in repairs for a house they might sell, Joe reframed it by noting the issue would surface in inspection, making the $1,784 immediate repair feel necessary rather than optional.

FIX — Schedule the Comfort Advisor appointment on-call while they're engaged with pricing; when cost hesitation hits, getting a specific callback date commits them to Option C rather than leaving the door open.

WIN — When customer objected to the $1,784 repair cost, you pivoted to booking the equipment specialist for a full system quote instead of defending the price. That repositioned the conversation from a painful immediate decision to a comparison of options, and the customer committed to the specialist appointment—that's the flip.

FIX — When customer expressed sticker shock at $7,900 repair, offer a bridge path: get the front unit working today for $815-1372, then schedule a Comfort Advisor follow-up for financing options and staged repairs, rather than deferring entirely to the competitor.

FIX — After you confirmed everything was working correctly, you had the perfect opening to present an upgrade path: 'I can get our comfort specialist to discuss garage insulation or a larger capacity unit to handle extreme heat better.' Instead, you ended at diagnosis. That's informative, but it leaves the Option C appointment on the table.
WIN — Clear explanation of system safety logic and commitment to comprehensive attic evaluation earned customer agreement to proceed; they trusted your expertise on the severity.
WIN — Tech acknowledged customer's frustration about repeated breakdowns and began setting expectations for comprehensive evaluation to identify root cause
FIX — When customer hesitates, reconnect to their stated concerns with empathy.

WIN — Tech demonstrated excellent patience with an elderly customer with hearing difficulty and set clear expectations for thorough evaluation despite customer's history of compressor replacement failures
FIX — When customer stated urgency ('just want to get it fixed'), schedule specialist visit for exact pricing instead of deferring to 'think about it'.

WIN — When customer reported capacitor failure and smoke, tech said 'I do a full evaluation of the situation,' immediately setting expectations and reassuring customer during initial safety-critical assessment

WIN — When customer stated they wanted replacement pricing not repairs for 1998 AC units, tech immediately called Comfort Advisor, recognizing customer intent and moving efficiently to the right specialist
WIN — Tech quickly established rapport and set clear expectations for a thorough evaluation despite the complex rental property ownership situation
FIX — When customer asked about R22 refrigerant costs, tech should have redirected to Option C and offered Comfort Advisor for replacement pricing instead of leaving customer uncertain

WIN — Tech thoroughly explained the R22 refrigerant cost issue (expired product at $600+ per pound), showed detailed pictures, presented membership savings on $4,600+ compressor replacement, and gave customer clear options to consider

WIN — Tech thoroughly explained system components, set clear expectations for inspection, and the customer remained engaged throughout the 155-minute call, leading to scheduling Comfort Advisor discussion
WIN — Tech quickly diagnosed the no-cooling situation and immediately offered to call Comfort Advisor for replacement options, moving customer to decision stage
FIX — Transcript too fragmented to assess coaching; requires audio review
WIN — Exceptional technical diagnosis with clear customer education on cascading failures

WIN — Tech stated 'I want to be thorough. I want to make sure I get everything. I want to get a full picture,' setting comprehensive expectations and the customer remained engaged and approved the extended evaluation
WIN — Tech clearly presented options for the 1-degree temperature variance, offered Option C replacement, let customers decide, and scheduled Comfort Advisor appointment for Monday discussion
WIN — Created next step that moves customer toward decision.

FIX — David's 10-minute tangent about flooring jobs and his family ate critical time before the options presentation; once he explained the capacitor issue, he should have refocused with 'Let me get you a quote on that repair,' moving the call toward the close instead of extending the diagnosis with technical stories.

WIN — Your car-battery analogy ('flip the ignition, cranks that motor') made the motor start device click for the customer, and when you offered the free specialist consult ('doesn't cost anything for them to come out'), they said yes to the $557 install plus the follow-up visit.

FIX — When customer expressed frustration about repeated previous repairs on multiple systems, tech should have recognized this as opening for Option C replacement and offered Comfort Advisor appointment for replacement discussion
